speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the nature of your vertigo—does the room spin around you, or do you feel like you are spinning—and did it start suddenly after a specific head movement?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the vertigo return if you roll over in bed or look up, and do you experience any hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or tinnitus?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any hearing loss, ringing in your ears, or fullness in one ear? Also, do you have any other neurological symptoms like double vision, slurred speech, or weakness in your limbs?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: You mentioned the vertigo lasted about 3 minutes and started as you were going to bed; does the spinning sensation return if you change your head position, such as rolling over or looking up? Also, can you confirm if you have any hearing changes or tinnitus in either ear?

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the vertigo is triggered by specific head movements and lasts less than a minute, I need to rule out central causes. I will now perform the Dix-Hallpike maneuver to check for nystagmus. REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Positive, inducing nystagmus and reproducing patient’s symptoms of vertigo when head is turned to the left and laid back.

speaker: Doctor
text: The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the left side confirms a peripheral cause. DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
